title: Ezekiel 27:12–25
context: The lament pauses for a long list of Tyre’s trading partners and wares (27:12–25), a single unit that runs from Tarshish in the far west to Arabia and Mesopotamia in the east. Silver, iron, tin, lead, horses, ivory, gems, grain, wine, wool, spices, and fine cloth all flow to the city, and the list closes with the ships of Tarshish carrying its goods (27:25). Many of the names also appear in the table of nations in Genesis 10. Identifications are offered with varying confidence, and some names remain uncertain. The list includes the trade in “the persons of men” (27:13), a sober reminder that the wealth celebrated in the poem included human beings. Judah and the land of Israel appear among the traders as well (27:17). Both traditions read the list as shared ground: it displays the scope of Tyre’s wealth just before the image of the ship returns and the wreck is described, and it shows the reach of the LORD’s judgment over a whole world of commerce.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Tarshish was your merchant by reason of the multitude of all kinds of riches. They traded for your wares with silver, iron, tin, and lead.
verses.arminianNotes: “Tarshish was your merchant by reason of the multitude of all kinds of riches,” trading silver, iron, tin, and lead. Tarshish was a distant port, often placed in the far west of the Mediterranean, though its location is debated. Arminian readers see the farthest reaches of the known world drawn to Tyre by its wealth and markets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list opening with the most distant trading partner to show that Tyre’s commerce encircled the known world, and the metals suggest the industries that fed its power. Shared ground: both traditions read the list as an inventory of glory that the lament will soon sink, and neither treats honest trade as sinful in itself.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech were your traders. They traded the persons of men and vessels of bronze for your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech” traded “the persons of men and vessels of bronze.” Javan is commonly linked with the Ionians and other peoples of the Aegean world, and Tubal and Meshech with regions of Asia Minor (compare Genesis 10:2). Arminian readers note soberly that human beings were treated as merchandise, and they hear an indictment within the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the trade in persons as a grave wrong set among ordinary goods, recalling the charges against Tyre in Amos 1:9 and Joel 3:4–6. Shared ground: both traditions hold that human beings bear God’s image (Genesis 1:27; 9:6), and both read the casual placement of slaves beside bronze as part of what makes the city’s wealth culpable.

verses.text: “ ‘ “They of the house of Togarmah traded for your wares with horses, war horses, and mules.
verses.arminianNotes: “They of the house of Togarmah traded for your wares with horses, war horses, and mules.” Togarmah appears in Genesis 10:3 and is often placed in eastern Asia Minor, though the identification is not certain. Arminian readers see the list moving through the peoples of the north, each bringing what its land produced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the horses and war horses point to military as well as commercial power flowing through Tyre’s markets. Shared ground: both traditions read the entry as one line in a single, sweeping list whose purpose is to display the reach of Tyre’s trade rather than to supply a precise map, and both hold the identification loosely.

verses.text: “ ‘ “The men of Dedan traded with you. Many islands were the market of your hand. They brought you horns of ivory and ebony in exchange.
verses.arminianNotes: “The men of Dedan traded with you,” and many islands brought “horns of ivory and ebony.” A Dedan appears among Arabian peoples (compare Genesis 25:3; Jeremiah 25:23), and another in the line of Cush (Genesis 10:7), so the reference here is uncertain. Arminian readers see exotic luxuries reaching Tyre from distant coasts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the ivory and ebony the kind of rare goods that marked royal splendor elsewhere in Scripture (compare 1 Kings 10:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the catalog of riches, and both treat the name Dedan here, which appears again in 27:20, with appropriate caution about which people is meant.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Syria was your merchant by reason of the multitude of your handiworks. They traded for your wares with emeralds, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Syria was your merchant by reason of the multitude of your handiworks,” trading emeralds, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies. Arminian readers note that Tyre’s own manufactured goods drew traders, and they see a city whose industry and skill were real gifts that became occasions for pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precious stones and fine cloth as part of the splendor that 28:13 will later echo in its own list of stones. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a two-way trade in luxury goods, and both hear in the abundance of handiwork the wealth that the lament treats as fleeting.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Judah and the land of Israel were your traders. They traded wheat of Minnith, confections, honey, oil, and balm for your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: “Judah and the land of Israel were your traders,” supplying wheat of Minnith, confections, honey, oil, and balm. Minnith appears in Judges 11:33 in the land of the children of Ammon. Arminian readers note that the LORD’s own people are named among Tyre’s partners, a reminder that the judgment falls on a world they were part of.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Judah and Israel supplying the produce of the land, the agricultural goods that Tyre, a city of the sea, needed (compare 1 Kings 5:11; Acts 12:20). Shared ground: both traditions read the entry as an ordinary trading relationship, not condemned in itself, and both see Israel’s presence in the list as placing Tyre’s fall within their own world.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Damascus was your merchant for the multitude of your handiworks by reason of the multitude of all kinds of riches, with the wine of Helbon, and white wool.
verses.arminianNotes: “Damascus was your merchant,” trading “the wine of Helbon, and white wool.” Helbon is often located in the hills near Damascus, though this is not certain. Arminian readers see the inland trade routes, as well as the sea lanes, converging on Tyre, so that its prosperity rested on the labor of many peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the piling up of phrases, “the multitude of your handiworks” and “all kinds of riches,” which presses home the sheer abundance of the city’s wealth. Shared ground: both traditions read the list’s accumulation of goods as a deliberate poetic effect that magnifies the greatness of what will be lost in the wreck.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Vedan and Javan traded with yarn for your wares; wrought iron, cassia, and calamus were among your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: “Vedan and Javan traded with yarn for your wares,” and wrought iron, cassia, and calamus were among the merchandise. Vedan is uncertain, and some readers think this Javan differs from the one in 27:13. Arminian readers see raw materials and aromatic goods alike passing through Tyre’s markets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that cassia appears among the ingredients of the holy anointing oil (compare Exodus 30:24), so that goods associated with worship in Israel were simply commodities in Tyre. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge the uncertainty of some names in the list, and both read the verse as part of the same catalog of wealth.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Dedan was your merchant in precious saddle blankets for riding.
verses.arminianNotes: “Dedan was your merchant in precious saddle blankets for riding.” Here Dedan is probably the Arabian people, whose caravans moved goods across the desert. Arminian readers see even specialized goods for riding reaching Tyre, a sign of how fully the city’s market met the desires of the wealthy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the brief entry as part of a turn toward Arabia and the east in verses 20–22, showing that Tyre’s commerce reached overland as well as by sea. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as one detail in the single list of 27:12–25, adding to the portrait of abundance, and both hold the geographical identification with some reserve.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your favorite dealers in lambs, rams, and goats. In these, they were your merchants.
verses.arminianNotes: “Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your favorite dealers in lambs, rams, and goats.” Kedar was a people of the Arabian desert (compare Isaiah 21:16–17; Jeremiah 49:28). Arminian readers see herding peoples supplying livestock, and the leaders of tribes eager to deal with Tyre.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word “princes” shows Tyre’s trade reaching the ruling classes of distant peoples, binding many leaders to its fortunes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the inventory of Tyre’s partners, and both see this wide dependence on Tyre as background to the grief of the kings and merchants in 27:33–36.

verses.text: “ ‘ “The traders of Sheba and Raamah were your traders. They traded for your wares with the best of all spices, all precious stones, and gold.
verses.arminianNotes: “The traders of Sheba and Raamah” brought “the best of all spices, all precious stones, and gold.” Sheba is commonly placed in southern Arabia (compare 1 Kings 10:1–2), and Raamah appears with Sheba in Genesis 10:7. Arminian readers see the most precious goods of the south flowing to Tyre.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear an echo of the queen of Sheba’s gifts to Solomon, though here the riches serve a city that glories in itself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the same catalog, adding the richest commodities to the list, and both hold the place identifications with appropriate caution.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Haran, Canneh, Eden, the traders of Sheba, Asshur and Chilmad, were your traders.
verses.arminianNotes: “Haran, Canneh, Eden, the traders of Sheba, Asshur and Chilmad, were your traders.” Haran is known from Genesis 11:31, and Asshur names Assyria. Canneh and Chilmad are uncertain, and this Eden is commonly taken as a place in Mesopotamia (compare 2 Kings 19:12). Arminian readers see the trade network reaching the river lands to the east.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the list, which began in the far west with Tarshish, now reaches the far east, so that Tyre seems to stand at the center of the world’s commerce. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing names as completing the circle of trade, and both distinguish this place from “Eden, the garden of God” in 28:13.

verses.text: These were your traders in choice wares, in wrappings of blue and embroidered work, and in cedar chests of rich clothing bound with cords, among your merchandise.
verses.arminianNotes: These traders dealt “in choice wares, in wrappings of blue and embroidered work, and in cedar chests of rich clothing bound with cords.” Arminian readers see the fine packaging and costly textiles as signs of a luxury trade in which presentation itself had value, and they hear the poem lingering over the details of wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detail as a final flourish before the list closes, giving the reader a vivid sense of the treasures that will soon be lost at sea. Shared ground: both traditions read the luxury goods as morally neutral in themselves while recognizing that they had become the substance of Tyre’s self-confidence and pride.

verses.text: “ ‘ “The ships of Tarshish were your caravans for your merchandise. You were replenished and made very glorious in the heart of the seas.
verses.arminianNotes: “The ships of Tarshish were your caravans for your merchandise. You were replenished and made very glorious in the heart of the seas.” The ship image returns. Arminian readers note that the phrase “the heart of the seas” recurs in 27:4, 26, and 27, binding glory and ruin to the same place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a hinge: Tyre’s fullness and glory reach their peak just before the storm of verse 26. Shared ground: both traditions read the sequence as a familiar biblical pattern of pride before a fall (compare Proverbs 16:18), and both see the closing line of the list as preparing the reader for the reversal.
